playbooks break here. This is where 12-month programs become 30-month programs.

The right posture right now is to hold the decision until three things resolve: the Oracle DB migration dependency, the CFO's capital posture signal, and the dependency sequencing on your on-prem stack. turns.label: Q9 pre-mortem
turns.query: Predict the 3 most likely reasons we fail to execute on your top recommendation.
turns.answer: The top recommendation from this session was kill or restructure AR-03, the Autonomous Customer Service Agent. Here are the three most likely failure modes if you don't act on it cleanly. First, the team renegotiates the goal instead of the initiative. Containment at 47% becomes "acceptable for this phase" and the target quietly shifts to 55%. This is the classic execution trap — the strategy was sound, the failure is in not letting the evidence drive the decision. You end up funding a third quarter of mediocre performance while the opportunity cost compounds. Second, ownership ambiguity stalls the call. The store-tech owner role vacancy I flagged earlier creates a real risk that no one has clear authority to pull the plug. Without a named decision-maker, this lives in committee indefinitely. Third, the AI Governance Council gate becomes a delay mechanism rather than a forcing function. If restructuring requires a governance sign-off and that body doesn't have a standing cadence for kill decisions — only for launches — the initiative drifts while the calendar fills up. The common thread: this isn't a capability failure, it's an organizational accountability failure. The fix is naming a decision owner, setting a 30-day hard deadline, and treating governance as a forcing function, not a buffer.
